sentences.text: The only known species of this genus is Majungasaurus crenatissimus.
It is distinguished by a wider skull, rough and thickened bone on the snout top, and a single rounded horn on the skull roof, featuring swollen, fused nasal bones and a frontal horn.
This theropod measured between 5.6 and 7.0 meters in length and weighed between 750 and 1100 kilograms, with some estimates placing its total length at 6 to 7 meters.
The genus was formerly known as Majungatholus, but this name is now considered a synonym of Majungasaurus.
Majungasaurus is the only dinosaur for which there is direct evidence of cannibalism.
Fossil evidence confirms Majungasaurus fed on the sauropod Rapetosaurus, leaving distinct tooth marks on its bones.
Majungasaurus appears to be more closely related to Indian abelisaurids than to those from South America or Africa.
Fossils were first found in 1896, though initially misidentified as Megalosaurus, and the genus was formally named by Lavocat in 1955.
All known fossils come from the Maevarano Formation in northwestern Madagascar, where 25 recorded fossil occurrences have been found.
Majungasaurus was a bipedal dinosaur with a long tail that balanced its head and torso, positioning its center of gravity over its hips.

Researchers suggest Majungasaurus used a 'bite-and-hold' feeding strategy similar to modern cats, relying on a short, broad snout to grip prey rather than slicing it, as it possessed an even broader snout than other abelisaurids.
Majungasaurus was the apex predator in its ecosystem, primarily hunting sauropods like Rapetosaurus, and was the largest carnivore and likely the dominant land predator in its environment.

Majungasaurus possessed pneumatic foramina in its vertebrae and ribs, suggesting it had an avian-style respiratory system with air sacs that allowed for highly efficient respiration where inhaled and exhaled air were not mixed.
The brain of Majungasaurus was very small relative to its body size and had a conservative structure closer to modern crocodilians than to birds.

A 2007 report was the first to examine pathologies in an abelisauroid dinosaur, noting that unlike tyrannosaurids which often show facial bite wounds, no wounds were found on any Majungasaurus skull elements.
Majungasaurus was among the slowest-growing theropod dinosaurs.
Throughout its ontogeny, the Majungasaurus skull, specifically the jugal, postorbital, and quadratojugal, became taller and more robust.
Researchers suggest that the unique skull shape of Majungasaurus indicates distinct hunting behaviors compared to other theropods.
A 2013 cladogram by Tortosa et al. places Majungasaurus in the new subfamily Majungasaurinae.

Recent analyses place Majungasaurus in a clade with Indian genera Rajasaurus and Indosaurus, excluding South American and African abelisaurids, suggesting separate clades in western and eastern Gondwana.
Majungasaurus lived in Madagascar between 70 and 66 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous Period.
Researchers debated whether the skull fragment originally named Majungatholus atopus belonged to Majungasaurus crenatissimus, initially judging the type dentary too fragmentary to link them.
Researchers suggest the skull horns and crests of Majungasaurus likely played a role in intraspecific competition, though their exact function remains unknown.
